title: Noor and Bram's Nighttime Mystery
markdown:
Noor the stoat was speedy as a blink. Her whiskers twitched at any sniff worth twitching for. Beetles. Berries. The good stuff at Willow Creek Allotments had a way of finding her nose first. Her best pal was Bram, a big gentle ram whose wool was fluffy as a cloud and whose bleats were deep rumbles. His curly horns gleamed as if someone polished them for show.

Every day was the same, and the same was mostly fine. Noor darted. Bugs nibbled. Bram munched clover. Prize pumpkins sat fat and pleased with themselves. The air smelled of damp soil, sweet peas, and sharp grass. Sometimes Noor’s nose found a hint of boring. Bram agreed with a rumbling baaaa. He secretly wished clover were not the whole of a life.

Then the sun laid gold stripes across dewdrops on the lettuce, and Noor zipped past the carrots and skidded. Her claws dug in.

“Bram! Look!”

A tiny bright blue flag stuck in the soil near her best carrots. It looked fairy-planted. Bram ambled over and peered down, brow furrowed.

“Baaaa. What’s this?”

“A flag,” Noor chirped, hopping. “Who put it there? Why?”

They hurried to Bram’s patch. More flags. Sunshine yellow by the plumpest tomatoes. Cheerful red by the strawberries. Someone had been decorating in the dark.

“A puzzler,” Noor declared.

Bram stroked his chin with a hoof. “Night decorator. Peculiar.”

A mischievous squirrel? A forgetful badger? A pixie with spare bunting? Noor puffed her chest. “We’ll have a night watch.” Her tummy did a wobbly flip all the same. Dark allotment. Long shadows. Sounds that did not introduce themselves. Bram nodded.

“Two pairs of eyes. My horns are… imposing.”

They hid among the huge pumpkin vines, a leafy hideout that smelled of orange and earth. The moon was a silver sliver. An owl hooted. Noor jumped and burrowed closer to Bram’s wool. The crickets went quiet, which was worse than the owl.

Then — rustle.

Noor’s heart thumped like a drum. Bram tensed, ready to bellow. A small shadowy figure darted from behind the shed, waddled, stooped by the pumpkins, set something down, and waddled away fast.

“A waddler,” Noor whispered. “They’re stealing pumpkins. The flags mark the route.”

Bram looked sceptical. “Taking nothing. Putting something down. And waddled. Hmm.”

Noor, scared and fast-thinking, was already sure. Sneaky thief.

Next morning they tiptoed the rows looking for crime. Nothing missing. Bram nudged a plump pumpkin. Still attached, still smug.

“But that waddler,” Noor said, grumpy now. “Up to no good.”

Bram kept glancing at the flags. Cheerful. Welcoming. Not thief-marks. More like an invitation written in cloth.

They tried again. Closer hideout. Noor, braver because being wrong had stung, spoke firm. “We need to see what they put down.”

“Maybe we’re looking wrong,” Bram said. “Not taking. Giving.”

Night. Owl. Heart-flips. Rustle. Waddle. The figure bent low, and Noor held her breath until it hurt.

Not a waddler. A hedgehog. Spines rustling. Placing plump slugs and snails in little piles by the carrots, the tomatoes, the strawberries. From a tiny pouch it took more flags and stuck them next to its dinner. Territory. A buffet. A map of snacks that would otherwise have been a map of chewed leaves.

Noor gasped, a tiny joyful sound. “It’s the hedgehog. It’s eating the pests. The flags show where.”

Bram’s chuckle ran through his wool. “Baaaa. The thief was a garden helper. Knew slugs were a menace. Gobbled them. Clever creature.”

The dark, which had been a thief’s country, became a place where help had feet. Noor’s whiskers settled. She had stayed. She had looked twice.

Ever since then they watch the allotments with wonder, not suspicion. They leave saucers of water for their prickly friend. The garden stays healthy, pest-chewed only in the polite places, bright with flags. And Noor greets each morning with a confident twitch, ready for whatever Willow Creek plants next.
characters: Noor (a speedy stoat), Bram (a gentle ram)
